Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
could you shape these notes into one clear geology field-notebook entry for the creek-cut visit, not a report or a conclusion about the site. keep it as a usable entry that someone can read later alongside the photographs and the scan. the date was 14 May 2024, and the stop was at the north bank of Alder Creek, about 300 metres east of the old Mill Road bridge. I started at 8:35 in the morning with Mara Chen. We were there to look at the exposed bank after the water dropped, not to collect a measured section. Put the date, place, people, and purpose near the start. The sky was bright but hazy, and the air was cool; no exact temperature was recorded, so please don't supply one. I wrote the location as approximate in my notebook, so don't turn that into a surveyed coordinate.

The exposure was roughly 2.4 metres high and about 11 metres long where we could see it from the path. Those are estimates, not measurements from a tape, and the path-side view did not show the full bank behind the willow roots. The lower half looked mostly gray-brown and finer grained than the upper part. There was a darker band near the middle, but its thickness changed along the face and was hard to follow where grass covered it. A pale, coarse patch appeared near the eastern end. We did not clear the plants or dig into the bank. Mention that limitation if it helps keep the description honest, but don't turn the visit into a claim about what lies below the visible surface.

At the western end, I saw thin, nearly flat layers, with a few small rusty-colored streaks. Toward the center, some layers seemed to dip slightly toward the creek, although the face is uneven and I didn't take a compass reading. Mara said, “that little ledge might be an old water line,” while we were looking at a step about halfway up the exposure. Keep her words as a quote and keep “might” in it; that was a suggestion while looking, not a confirmed interpretation. We did not decide whether the step was caused by erosion, a change in sediment, or something else. Don't settle that question in the entry.

There were a few rounded pebbles in the coarser material, most around 1 to 3 centimetres across by eye, and two larger ones that I estimated at about 5 centimetres. I noticed a milky quartz pebble and one reddish pebble, but I did not identify the reddish one beyond its color. No sample was taken, and there are no lab results. A thin twig lay across one part of the dark band, which makes the band harder to see in the photo from the path. I want the notebook entry to separate what we actually observed from what we guessed, without making it sound like we identified every grain or pebble.

I have three image files for this stop, photo_17.jpg, photo_18.jpg, and photo_19.jpg, plus the scanned page scan_17.tif. They are the files associated with this entry, and do not rename files. The first photo shows most of the exposure with Mara's yellow ruler held near the lower edge for scale; the ruler was not used to measure the whole bank. The second is closer on the central step and the dark band, and the twig crosses the lower right corner. The third looks east toward the pale coarse patch, with willow roots at the top edge. The scan is a page of my handwritten field notes, not a map. Refer to the files by their existing names if you mention them, and make clear which view each one shows.

For the measurements and estimated dimensions, it may be easiest to make a short numbered section rather than burying everything in prose. The exposure height estimate is 2.4 metres; visible length estimate is 11 metres; pebble estimates are 1 to 3 centimetres for most and about 5 centimetres for the two larger ones. The stop was around 300 metres east of the bridge. Please keep “about,” “roughly,” or another clear estimate marker wherever those values are described. The yellow ruler in photo_17.jpg is only a visual scale cue near the lower edge and does not change how we obtained the exposure dimensions. I didn't record a dip angle, a compass bearing, or a precise location, so don't add any of those.

We also noted that the creek was low enough to expose the bank face, but I did not write down a water height or compare it with an earlier visit. The toe of the bank was damp, while the upper face looked dry from the path. There were willow roots at the top and grass obscuring part of the dark band. The bank face appeared intact during our visit; we did not see a fresh slump, though that only describes what we could see at that time. Keep the statement tied to this visit rather than making it a general claim about bank stability. I didn't photograph the creek bed itself, so don't imply the image set covers it.

Please keep the sequence of the visit sensible: identify the stop and purpose, describe the visible exposure from west toward east, then give the pebble and layer observations, and finish with the file references and limits of what we could infer. You can smooth the rough wording and use headings that suit a field notebook, but keep it as one entry, not separate entries for each image. A short numbered measurements section is fine. Avoid turning the quote into a finding or adding a rock name, age, depositional setting, or explanation that is not in these notes. I need the entry to remain useful as a record of what we saw on that morning, including what we didn't measure or sample.

One last detail for the entry: we left the stop at 9:20, and a light breeze came up while we were packing. The path was muddy near the bridge on the walk back, but that was away from the exposure and wasn't part of the bank description. Keep the leaving time and the breeze as visit details if there is a natural place for them. Don't present the muddy path as evidence about the creek bank. The notebook page had no follow-up plan written on it, and I don't want one added. End with that visit information rather than a summary judgment about the site.", "output": "Turn the notes below into one clear, usable geology field-notebook entry for the creek-cut visit. Keep it as an entry, not a report or a conclusion about the site. Smooth the wording and use suitable headings, but preserve the observations, estimates, uncertainties, and limits in the notes. Arrange the information in this order: identify the stop and purpose; describe the visible exposure from west toward east; record the pebble and layer observations; then give file references and limits on interpretation. A short numbered section for measurements and estimated dimensions is appropriate. Keep this as one entry, not separate entries for each image.

Include the date, place, people, and purpose near the beginning: 14 May 2024, north bank of Alder Creek, about 300 metres east of the old Mill Road bridge, with Mara Chen, starting at 8:35 a.m. The visit was to look at the exposed bank after the water dropped, not to collect a measured section. The sky was bright but hazy and the air cool; no exact temperature was recorded. The location is approximate, not a surveyed coordinate.

Describe the exposure as roughly 2.4 metres high and about 11 metres long where visible from the path. These are estimates, not tape measurements, and the path-side view did not show the full bank behind the willow roots. The lower half looked mostly gray-brown and finer grained than the upper part. A darker band near the middle varied in thickness and was difficult to follow where grass covered it. A pale, coarse patch appeared near the eastern end. The plants were not cleared and the bank was not dug into, so do not claim anything about what lies below the visible surface.

At the western end, the layers were thin and nearly flat, with a few small rusty-colored streaks. Toward the center, some layers seemed to dip slightly toward the creek, but the face was uneven and no compass reading was taken. Preserve Mara’s quote about the step halfway up the exposure exactly in substance: “that little ledge might be an old water line.” Keep “might”; it was a suggestion, not a confirmed interpretation. The cause of the step was not determined. Do not decide whether it resulted from erosion, a sediment change, or something else.

Record that the coarser material contained a few rounded pebbles, most estimated by eye at 1 to 3 centimetres across, and two larger ones estimated at about 5 centimetres. One pebble was milky quartz; another was reddish, but was not identified beyond its color. No sample was taken and there are no lab results. A thin twig lay across part of the dark band and makes it harder to see in the path-side photograph. Distinguish observations from guesses, without implying that every grain or pebble was identified.

Use a short numbered section for these approximate dimensions and distances:
1. Exposure height: roughly 2.4 metres.
2. Visible exposure length: about 11 metres.
3. Most pebbles: estimated at 1 to 3 centimetres; two larger pebbles: about 5 centimetres.
4. Stop location: about 300 metres east of the old Mill Road bridge.

Keep the estimate markers with the values. The yellow ruler visible near the lower edge of photo_17.jpg is only a visual scale cue; it was not used to measure the whole bank and does not change how the exposure dimensions were obtained. Do not add a dip angle, compass bearing, or precise location.

Refer to the associated files by their existing names: photo_17.jpg, photo_18.jpg, photo_19.jpg, and scan_17.tif. For the image and scan files listed here, do not rename files. photo_17.jpg shows most of the exposure, with Mara’s yellow ruler near the lower edge; photo_18.jpg is a closer view of the central step and dark band, with the twig crossing the lower right corner; photo_19.jpg looks east toward the pale coarse patch, with willow roots at the top edge. scan_17.tif is a scan of the handwritten field-notebook page, not a map. Make clear which view each image shows if you refer to the files.

Include the other visit observations with their limits. The creek was low enough to expose the bank face, but no water height was recorded and no comparison with an earlier visit was made. The bank toe was damp; the upper face looked dry from the path. Willow roots were at the top, and grass obscured part of the dark band. The face appeared intact during this visit, and no fresh slump was seen; keep that statement limited to what was visible at the time, not a general claim about bank stability. The creek bed itself was not photographed, so do not imply that the image set covers it.

End with the visit details: the stop was left at 9:20, and a light breeze came up while packing. The path was muddy near the bridge on the walk back, away from the exposure; do not present that as evidence about the creek bank. No follow-up plan was written on the notebook page, and none should be added. Do not add a rock name, age, depositional setting, or explanation that is absent from the notes. Finish with the visit information, not a summary judgment about the site."}]
